summary: This standards-track memo specifies two transport mappings of the RAQMON information model from RFC 4710. One uses TCP as a native transport and the other uses SNMP, to carry data from a RAQMON Data Source to a RAQMON Report Collector. It was later updated by RFC 8996.

plainLanguage.summary: Quality reports need a delivery truck. This picks two kinds of trucks, TCP and SNMP, for carrying reports from a gadget to the collector.

subtitle: The binary report format for RAQMON quality monitoring, plus how to carry it over TCP with TLS or over SNMP notifications.

tldr.problem: RAQMON (RFC 4710) defines what quality-of-service metrics a data source reports to a collector, but devices also need an exact wire format and a way to deliver the reports.
tldr.mechanism: The memo defines the RAQMON PDU, a BASIC part with a presence-flag word plus optional vendor extensions, and maps it onto TCP (secured with StartTLS) or onto SNMP notifications through the RAQMON-RDS-MIB.
tldr.outcome: Collectors MUST support the TCP transport and MAY support SNMP. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4712 is a Proposed Standard and was later updated by RFC 8996. It builds on the framework in RFC 4710.

sections.title: What This Memo Adds to RAQMON
sections.content:
The RAQMON framework of RFC 4710 extends the RMON family of monitoring protocols. It defines RAQMON Data Sources (RDS) that measure application quality and RAQMON Report Collectors (RRC) that receive the reports. RFC 4710 defines the metrics. This memo supplies the syntax of the common protocol data unit (PDU) and the transports that carry it.

A RAQMON PDU does not transport application data. It sits in the place of a payload specification at the application layer. Implementers get two transport choices, but RRCs MUST implement the TCP transport and MAY implement the SNMP transport.
sections.plainLanguage: A quality report needs a form to fill in and a way to send it. This RFC gives the form and two ways to deliver it, and says the collector must always accept the main way.

sections.title: The BASIC Part of the PDU
sections.content:
A PDU is sent as one unit but has two functional parts: the BASIC part and optional application extensions. The current version is marked PDT = 1. Vendors MUST use the BASIC part for the parameters listed in the specification, and MAY use extensions for others.

The first word holds PDT (5 bits), B (1 bit, 1 means a BASIC part is present), T (3 bits, the number of application extensions that follow), P (padding), S and R (set when the source or receiver address is IPv6), RC (4 bits) and a 16-bit length in 32-bit words minus one. Next comes the 32-bit DSRC, which identifies one reporting session and should be generated randomly for each session.

After the SMI enterprise code (0 for the BASIC format), the report type and RC_N, a 32-bit set of RAQMON Parameter Presence Flags says which parameters follow. Bits 0 to 31 stand for items such as source address, receiver address, NTP timestamp, delays, packet counts, jitter and loss fraction. Only flagged parameters appear, so a PDU stays small. Padding of 0, 8, 16 or 24 bits keeps the BASIC part a multiple of 32 bits.

A PDU with B and T both zero is a NULL PDU and ends with the DSRC field. RDSs MUST send one to signal the end of a reporting session. The sub-session number RC_N is 8 bits, so one packet can describe at most 256 records.
sections.plainLanguage: The report starts with a checklist saying which boxes are filled in, so you only send the answers that matter. A blank form with a special mark means the report is finished.

sections.title: Parameter Encodings
sections.content:
Each parameter refers back to a section of RFC 4710 and has a fixed size. Addresses are 32 bits for IPv4 or 160 bits for IPv6. The session setup time is a 64-bit NTP timestamp. Round-trip and one-way delay, session duration and the packet and octet counters are 32 bits each. Ports are 16 bits. Session setup delay, application delay, delay variation and inter-arrival jitter are 16 bits, in milliseconds.

Text parameters (application name, data source name, receiver name, setup status) start with an 8-bit octet count followed by UTF-8 text, padded to a multiple of 32 bits. The data source and receiver names MUST NOT exceed 255 octets and should be sent only occasionally, because they stay constant for a session.

Priority and utilization values are one octet: layer 2 priority uses the first 3 bits for the IEEE 802.1 tag with the remaining 5 bits zero, and CPU and memory utilization are percentages from 0 to 100. Loss and discard fractions are 8-bit fixed-point numbers with the binary point at the left edge. All integers are in network byte order and header data is aligned to its natural length.
sections.plainLanguage: Every answer box on the form has a fixed size, like a box for a number of seconds or a box for a name. Names start with a count of letters so the reader knows where they end.

sections.title: Vendor Extensions (APP Part)
sections.content:
The APP part lets new applications add data without registering a new PDU type. Each extension starts with an SMI enterprise code, a report type and a length. A non-zero enterprise code marks a vendor- or application-specific extension, and one PDU can carry several of them.

Any RAQMON-compliant RRC MUST recognise vendors' enterprise codes and MUST recognise the presence of extensions by their report types. It does not need to understand what they mean, because the application-dependent data is interpreted by the vendor-specific application. Vendors are RECOMMENDED to publish their extensions and report types.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a blank page at the back of the form where a company can add its own questions. The collector knows a page is there, even if it cannot read the company's questions.

sections.title: Securing a TCP Session with StartTLS
sections.content:
Over TCP, a session can be protected with TLS. The RDS client sends a TLS_REQ PDU after the TCP connection is up and MUST NOT send other PDUs until it gets a TLS_RESP. The RRC MUST answer with a one-octet result code: 0 OK, 1 OP_ERR, 2 PROTO_ERR, 3 UNAVAIL, 4 CONF_REQD, 5 STRONG_AUTH_REQD or 6 REFERRAL.

On success the client MUST either begin a TLS negotiation or close the connection. Afterwards both sides MUST individually decide whether the achieved security level is enough. The client MUST check the server's hostname against the dNSName in the certificate's subjectAltName, and a wildcard character applies only to the left-most name component. The RDS client authenticates the RRC, and the RRC optionally authenticates the RDS, though the server MUST authenticate the client when the deployment is exposed to spoofing.

Either side MAY close TLS gracefully with a closure alert, which leaves the RAQMON connection intact, or abruptly by dropping the TCP connection.
sections.plainLanguage: Before sending secrets, the sender knocks and asks, "Can we use a locked tunnel?" The collector says yes, no, or try somewhere else, and both sides check the tunnel is strong enough before talking.

sections.title: Sending RAQMON over SNMP
sections.content:
SNMP notifications were chosen so that devices already running SNMP agents can act as RDSs. The memo warns that SNMP uses UDP, so congestion is more likely, and that its encoding is less efficient. It therefore RECOMMENDS TCP where available, RECOMMENDS Inform PDUs, does NOT RECOMMEND Traps, and RECOMMENDS keeping notifications within the MTU size to avoid fragmentation.

The RAQMON-RDS-MIB module MUST be used to map PDUs onto notifications. Its notification table is indexed by the DSRC, the sub-session number and the peer address, and application extensions travel as additional variable bindings. When Inform PDUs are used, the RDS MUST process the responses and MUST limit the number of PDUs sent per time interval. Standard UDP port 162 SHOULD be used. Implementers using SNMP over UDP MUST follow the congestion-safety measures in section 3 of RFC 4710.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP is a second, lighter way to send the report, using devices that already know how to send alerts. It is like sending a postcard instead of a registered letter, so the RFC prefers the registered letter.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 4710 sets out the threat model. This memo asks that implementations offer authentication, privacy, protection from denial-of-service attacks on the RRC, and NAT and firewall friendliness. For TCP, TLS MUST be used. To limit DoS, an RDS sends the first report only after the session is established. Where NAT is a concern, the RDS MAY omit IP address information.

For the MIB module, no object is read-write or read-create, so SNMP SET cannot alter or create its objects. The notification table holds user session information that can be sensitive, and SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, so implementers are RECOMMENDED to consider the SNMPv3 security features.
sections.plainLanguage: Reports say who talked to whom, so they must be kept private, and the collector must not be flooded with fake reports. Use the locked tunnel for TCP and the safer version of SNMP.

sections.title: Port Number and OID
sections.content: Port 7744 is registered with IANA as the default port for RAQMON PDUs over TCP. It was chosen above 5000 to fit Unix practice, where privileged processes use ports below 1024 and the operating system assigns ports from 1024 to 5000. Hosts running several applications may provision a separate TCP port instead. The OID for the MIB module is assigned under RFC 3737, so no IANA action is needed for it.
sections.plainLanguage: Collectors listen at a well-known door number, 7744, so devices know where to knock.

fields.desc: Number of application extensions that follow.

fields.desc: Padding present at end of BASIC part.

fields.desc: Application records in the BASIC part.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: BASIC part length in 32-bit words minus one.

fields.desc: Zero for the BASIC part format.

fields.desc: Zero for the PDU version in this document.

fields.name: Parameter Presence Flags
fields.desc: One bit per optional parameter that follows.

viz.caption: STARTTLS ON A RAQMON TCP CONNECTION

messages.label: TLS_REQ
messages.note: Sent after the TCP connection is established; no other PDUs until the response.

messages.label: TLS_RESP (Result)
messages.note: 0 OK, or an error such as PROTO_ERR or UNAVAIL.

messages.label: TLS negotiation
messages.note: On success the client begins TLS or closes the connection.

items.label: OK
items.desc: Success. The server is willing and able to negotiate TLS.

items.label: OP_ERR
items.desc: Sequencing error, for example TLS already established.

items.label: PROTO_ERR
items.desc: TLS not supported or incorrect PDU format.

items.label: UNAVAIL
items.desc: TLS service problem or RRC server going down.

items.label: REFERRAL
items.desc: Referral to an RRC server supporting TLS.
